name: The Republic
info: The Republic is a Socratic dialogue by Plato, written around 375 BCE, in which Socrates and others ask what justice is and describe a hypothetical just city ruled by philosopher-kings; it became a founding work of political philosophy.

facts.made: Plato, who wrote it as a Socratic dialogue around 375 BCE; its speakers include Socrates, Glaucon, Adeimantus, Cephalus, Polemarchus and Thrasymachus
facts.form: A dialogue in ten books, in Ancient Greek (Politeia), on justice, the just city-state and the just man
facts.where: Read in editions and translations; fragments of it are among the Oxyrhynchus Papyri, and a different version was found in 1945 in the Nag Hammadi library
facts.known: Kallipolis; philosopher-kings; the Ring of Gyges; the noble lie; the Ship of State; the Sun, the Divided Line and the allegory of the cave; the myth of Er

t: Plato's dialogue asks whether the just man is happier than the unjust man, and builds a hypothetical city, Kallipolis, ruled by philosopher-kings, to see how justice comes to be in the soul.
It compares five kinds of regime, aristocracy, timocracy, oligarchy, democracy and tyranny, and the kinds of soul that correspond to them.
Readers have disagreed from the 20th century onward over whether Plato meant the city as a political programme, an ironic exercise or an analogy for the individual soul.
dyk: The English title comes from Cicero's De re publica, written about three centuries later, and is not an exact translation of Plato's Greek title Politeia, a general term for the actual and possible forms of government of a city-state.
ev: Plato writes the Republic, a dialogue on justice, the just city-state and the just man
Oxyrhynchus papyrus fragments containing parts of the Republic are written, between about 200 and 300 CE
A different version of the Republic is copied in the Nag Hammadi library
John Burnet publishes the Greek text in his Platonis opera
Karl Popper's The Open Society and Its Enemies singles out Plato's state as a dystopia, and fragments of a different version are discovered at Nag Hammadi
Simon R. Slings publishes a new Oxford edition of the Greek text

sections.origins:
The Republic (Ancient Greek Politeia, Latin De Republica) is a Socratic dialogue that Plato wrote around 375 BCE. It concerns justice (dikaiosune), the order and character of the just city-state, and the just man. Its setting seems to be the time of the Peloponnesian War. The conversation begins when Socrates and Glaucon visit Athens' port, Piraeus, and are intercepted by Polemarchus, who demands that they join him for a dinner and festival. At Polemarchus' house Socrates meets Polemarchus' father, Cephalus.

The work is generally placed in the middle period of Plato's dialogues, although the line between the middle and early dialogues is less clear than the line between the late dialogues and all the others. Ritter, Arnim and Baron, each using a separate method, agree that the Republic stood apart, along with Parmenides, Phaedrus and Theaetetus. The first book shares many features with earlier dialogues and is thought to have been written first as a separate work, with the remaining books joined to it, perhaps with changes to the first book.

The English title derives from Cicero's De re publica, but res publica is not an exact translation of politeia, a general term for the actual and potential forms of government for a polis.
sections.content:
In Book I Socrates asks Cephalus about old age and the definition of justice; Cephalus holds that justice is honesty and returning what is owed, Polemarchus that it is doing good to friends and harm to enemies, and Thrasymachus that it is whatever is advantageous for the stronger. Socrates answers each in turn. In Book II Glaucon tells the story of Gyges, who uses a ring that makes him invisible to gain advantages by injustice, and asks Socrates to defend justice as good in itself. Socrates proposes to use a city as an image of the soul, and describes a healthy city of producers, then a luxurious one that needs a guardian class.

The later books set out Kallipolis, the just city. The guardians receive a censored education, are forbidden private property, and are told a noble lie, the myth of the metals. Justice is defined as each class doing its own work, matched by a soul of rational, spirited and appetitive parts. Philosophers, who know the Forms, are to rule; the Sun, the Divided Line and the allegory of the cave illustrate the Form of the Good. Book VIII traces decline from aristocracy through timocracy, oligarchy and democracy to tyranny, and Book X ends with the myth of Er.
sections.making:
The Republic is a dialogue, in which Socrates discusses justice with various Athenians and foreigners. It is divided into ten books, and the passages are cited by the numbers of the Stephanus pagination, such as 327a for the start of Book I and 621d for the end of Book X. Plato wrote it around 375 BCE. The first book is thought to have been composed as a separate work and joined to the rest, perhaps with changes.

Its arrangement has been described in different ways. Eric Voegelin saw an introduction and conclusion that frame a main body, with the Prologue in Book I, a short dialogue on common opinions about justice, and the Epilogue in Book X, which he said rests on faith and not reason and describes the new arts and the immortality of the soul. The main body, in his reading, has three parts, the establishment of the economic and social orders of a polis, the embodiment of the idea of the city, and the analysis of its decline.

Within the text Socrates works by refutation and by analogy: he answers each definition of justice in Book I with a counter-example or argument, and later offers images such as the Ship of State, the Sun, the Divided Line and the cave. In Book IV he sets the parts of the city beside the parts of the soul, and in Book VIII Plato's number is mentioned enigmatically.
sections.reception:
Aristotle systematised many of Plato's analyses in his Politics and criticised the proposals of several political philosophers for the ideal city-state. Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism, wrote a Republic of his own in opposition to Plato's, which some later Stoics viewed with embarrassment because of its defences of free love, incest and cannibalism. Cicero's De re publica, about three centuries later, imitates Plato's style and treats many of the same topics, though its discussion centres more on improving the Roman Republic. Augustine of Hippo described an ideal city of his own, the eternal Jerusalem, in his City of God.

Islamic philosophers were more interested in Aristotle than in Plato, and Ibn Rushd (Averroes), without access to Aristotle's Politics, wrote a commentary on the Republic. He took up its ideal of a monarchy led by a philosopher-king, its equality of women, who should be educated and serve in the military, and its censorship of literature. Thomas More's Utopia shares with the Republic common property and the lack of privacy. Hegel held that Plato had grasped the spirit of his own time and wrote the Republic as an attempt to keep out the new freedom of private property.
sections.survival:
Several Oxyrhynchus Papyri fragments were found to contain parts of the Republic, along with parts of other works such as Phaedo and Gorgias, written around 200 to 300 CE. Fragments of a different version of the Republic were discovered in 1945 as part of the Nag Hammadi library, written about 350 CE. These finds are taken to show the influence of Plato in Egypt in those times.

The work later reached English readers through translations, among them J. L. Davies and D. J. Vaughan in 1852, George Burges in 1854, Benjamin Jowett in 1871, H. D. P. Lee in 1955, Allan Bloom in 1991, Robin Waterfield in 1994, Tom Griffith in 2000, R. E. Allen in 2006, Joe Sachs in 2007 and Christopher Rowe in 2012. Jowett's translation is available as an e-text from Project Gutenberg, and Paul Shorey's of 1935 with the Greek on the Perseus Project. The standard Greek texts named include John Burnet's Platonis opera of 1902 and Simon R. Slings' edition of 2003. A public-domain audiobook of the Republic is available at LibriVox, and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy carry articles on it.
sections.legacy:
Readers in the 20th century drew very different conclusions. Mussolini admired the Republic and often read it for inspiration, and it contains ideas that fascism promoted, such as rule by an elite and the militarisation of a nation through a class of warriors, though Plato was an idealist focused on justice and morality, while fascism was realist, focused on political goals. Martin Luther King Jr. named the Republic as the one book, apart from the Bible, that he would want on a desert island.

Critics disagreed on its purpose. Karl Popper, in The Open Society and Its Enemies of 1945, called Plato's state a totalitarian dystopia and held that it was meant as a topical political manifesto; Bertrand Russell argued that it was meant as a practical form of government, and G. A. Cohen that it was not totalitarian in the strict sense. Gadamer, Leo Strauss and Allan Bloom read it as a heuristic utopia or a learning exercise, and Voegelin considered Popper's reading a gross misunderstanding. Others read the city as an analogy for the individual soul. Aldous Huxley's Brave New World has been compared to it, and Louis Andriessen composed De Staat on its text in the early 1970s.

summary: The Republic is Plato's Socratic dialogue of about 375 BCE on justice, in which Socrates and others describe a hypothetical just city ruled by philosopher-kings and compare it with the soul. It was taken up by later philosophers and remains disputed as to its purpose.
notes: The article gives no date for the writing beyond 'around 375 BC' and gives Plato's Academy/dating context nothing further.

The article gives no dates for Aristotle, Ibn Rushd, More or Cicero (only 'some three centuries later'), so they are not in the key events. The Nag Hammadi find is dated 1945 and its copy c. 350 CE by the article.
Article's 'Stephanus numbers' appear only in the external links note; the pagination reference is as the article's book headings give it.
Left out: the 2001 and 2021 surveys ranking the book, the films and novels that use it.
